issues.title: The mind is not a camera
issues.subject_candidate: The mind is not a camera
issues.preheader_candidate: A stranger changed mid-conversation. What can a witness actually claim?
issues.excerpt_candidate: Imagine describing a conversation with complete confidence—then discovering the person across from you had changed. A real-world change-blindness experiment shows why attention and accuracy aren't the same thing. Its findings concern a particular experiment, not a universal failure rate for eyewitnesses. This edition offers a practical way to separate an observation from an inference. Read the full investigation and inspect the source for yourself.

issues.title: Before hypnosis had a name
issues.preheader_candidate: A report from 1784 is fascinating—and not the same thing as proof.
issues.excerpt_candidate: On May 4, 1784, Puységur described an encounter that seemed to challenge ordinary explanations. He wrote about it four days later. The first question isn't whether his theory was true; it's what the record actually permits us to say. This edition compares testimony, retrospective claims and what independent corroboration would require. Read the evidence trail before deciding what the story means.

issues.title: Apollo 1 and the unproven spark
issues.subject_candidate: Apollo 1: why one spark was never the whole story
issues.preheader_candidate: NASA's record distinguishes radio silence, speech and the causes it could establish.
issues.excerpt_candidate: The final Apollo 1 radio record covers about 17.1 seconds, but not 17.1 seconds of continuous speech—and not the fire's entire duration. NASA's investigators could describe the dangerous system even without definitively locating a single ignition source. We examine the cabin atmosphere, materials, hatch and the uncomfortable difference between evidence and a tidy explanation. Read the investigation, then follow the primary source.
